doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: Why Hamilton alumni stay loyal, compared with Michigan
summary: He explains the Hamilton attitude towards students compared with Ann Arbor, and praises Gene Tobin and Joe Anderson.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Well I wanted to talk a little bit more about your faithfulness and your support of Hamilton College and I’m impressed by the group of men from your class and from others back then who have had a lifelong commitment to this college. Can you explain why?

I’ve often wondered. The people here did a terrific job of injecting us all with some kind of fluid. We came out of here thinking Hamilton is a wonderful place, and we never changed that viewpoint. I can’t understand for example my own kids, who went to other schools, which I would consider the same kind of school, small and so on, and they don’t give a damn. They don’t give them any money, they don’t care. I just don’t understand, I say why don’t you ever go back? They’re just not interested. They got an education and they got out. I could give you an example of the difference I think. When the war ended, this college took Carnegie Dorm and converted it to apartments for veterans with wives. So each one of the three man apartments was equipped with a dish cupboard and a refrigerator and a stove and so on. And they practically gave those to us when we came back. I lived in one the summer I was here. They put a laundry under Buttrick, and we all moved in. There was 24 couples over there in that building, and we had a hell of a time. And then they built the Village, which has now been removed, back of the Alpha Delta house. So they had a concern for us okay? I left there and I went one day out to Michigan. I went to Ann Arbor, registered for the law school and said now where do I live? Huh? And I had a hell of a time. In the middle of the winter we moved three times in that damn town, and ended up in a scummy place where I spent the rest of the three years. But the point was nobody cared. Nobody cared. And you were a number. My classes were as big as the whole college here. And I must say I did well in school. I became very friendly with the professors, I was a member of the honor society that threw all the drunken parties and stuff, so I knew them better than most, but I still have no regard for that school at all. I’ve never been back. I’ve never given them any money and I’m just not interested. So there’s a difference. It’s an attitude I think, towards the students. I mean here, my freshman year every second Saturday my roommate and I would go to Utica and have a spaghetti dinner with two professors, and just talk and come back. It’s a totally different attitude. Totally different experience. And as a result of that experience I insisted that my kids at least start off in a small liberal arts college and get at least two years rather than have to go face the crowd. And the other day we drove

down to Ithaca and toured Cornell. My God. You can’t even move. You can’t park your car, you can’t do anything. And I thought what a difference, what a difference. I think it’s the type of college, and I’d be surprised if it isn’t duplicated in schools like Williams and Amherst and so on. I think it’s the attitude and the life you lead with the school, the relationship between you and the school. The fact that, Gene Tobin has a thing over here every week for the kids to come talk to him. I mean that doesn’t exist in other schools. I think that’s what makes a difference. And I don’t think it’s our class alone. We were very high on the list of graduate donors to our alumni fund, nationally. We’re in the first ten I think. And we have a good — that’s what makes this college is the alumni.
